title: The Potter in 120,000 Beads
text: On the mangrove edge of the Bang Pakong River, a woman who probably died in her 30s was buried in garments stitched with more than 120,000 shell disc beads. Beside her ankle lay a potter's anvil and burnishing stones, so archaeologist Charles Higham thinks she was a specialist potter. A baby buried nearby had a miniature clay anvil of its own.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Ochre use in burial practices in Thailand, from the Neolithic to the Iron Age

source2.name: World Archaeology: Charles Higham, A prehistoric mystery

title: Rowing Souls on a Burial Jar
place: Manunggul Cave, Lipuun Point, Palawan, Philippines
text: In Manunggul Cave on Palawan, people used this earthenware jar about 2,700 years ago to protect the remains of the dead. On its lid, two small figures sit in a boat: the souls of the dead rowing their way to the afterlife. The jar shows a society that believed in the soul and life after death thousands of years before contact with organized religions.

source.name: Cultural Center of the Philippines Encyclopedia of Philippine Art: Manunggul Jar

title: A New Capital Across the River
text: In 1782 General Chao Phraya Chakkri took the throne as Rama I and moved the court of Siam from the west to the east bank of the Chao Phraya River. A wide bend in the river formed a natural moat, while to the east lay a swampy delta called the Sea of Mud. Rama I modeled his new city on the former capital, Ayutthaya.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Bangkok

title: Francis Light Lands on Penang
text: In 1786 Captain Francis Light of the British East India Company founded Fort Cornwallis on the island of Penang. The town that grew around it, George Town, flourished as a port of call on the India-China shipping run and drew Hokkien, Cantonese and Indian traders. Its shophouses and religious buildings of many faiths are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: George Town, Malaysia

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Melaka and George Town, Historic Cities of the Straits of Malacca

title: Sugar and Coffee Instead of Rice
text: In 1830 Governor-General Johannes van den Bosch introduced the Culture System in the Dutch East Indies. Javanese villagers were meant to set aside one-fifth of their rice fields for export crops such as sugar, coffee and indigo, or work 66 days for the government. In practice farmers lost more land and labor than that, and were left responsible when crops failed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Culture System

title: A Fever Dream of Evolution
text: Towards the end of February 1858, after a serious attack of malaria, naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace wrote an essay on how varieties of living things can drift away from their original type. He dated it from Ternate in the Moluccas and mailed it to Charles Darwin, who had reached the same idea independently. Their papers were read together in London on July 1, 1858.

source.name: Darwin Online: Darwin and Wallace 1858, On the tendency of species to form varieties (Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society)

source2.name: Mètode (Universitat de València), Xavier Bellés: The naturalist who got ahead of Darwin

title: The Fall of a Greek Courtier
text: Constantine Phaulkon sailed to Siam as a boy, learned Thai quickly, and rose to become King Narai's leading minister, inviting French troops and missionaries in. When Narai fell seriously ill in 1688, an anti-French faction led by the king's foster brother Phetracha overthrew him. Phaulkon was executed at Lop Buri, the French garrisons were expelled, and the new king, Phetracha, limited foreign influence.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Constantine Phaulkon

title: The Last Prau to Marege
text: From at least 1700, hundreds of fishermen sailed each December from Makassar to northern Australia, a coast they called Marege, to catch, boil and dry trepang (sea cucumber) for sale to China. They brought Yolŋu people metal knives and axes, tobacco and words such as rrupia (money). After 1901 Australia banned the trepangers, and in 1907 the last prau made the voyage.

source.name: National Museum of Australia: Trade with the Makasar

title: The Han Swallow Nam Viet
text: Nam Viet, or Southern Yue, was a kingdom stretching from southern China across the Red River delta as far south as Da Nang. In 111 BCE the Han emperor Wu Ti conquered it. Chinese settlement and culture followed into northern Vietnam, but the attempt to absorb Vietnam into China also made its people increasingly aware of their own identity.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nam Viet

title: Roman Envoys Arrive by Vietnam
text: According to China's Book of the Later Han, in 166 CE envoys sent by Andun, king of Da Qin (the Roman Empire under Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), arrived through Rinan on the central Vietnamese coast. They offered elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn and turtle shell. The chronicler grumbled that the gifts were neither precious nor rare, raising suspicion that the accounts might be exaggerated.

source.name: Silk Road Seattle (University of Washington): The Western Regions according to the Hou Hanshu, trans. John E. Hill

title: Sultan Agung Marches on Batavia
text: Sultan Agung of Mataram brought his central Javanese kingdom to its greatest power, subduing coastal states from Tuban to Surabaya. Openly contemptuous of trade, he kept no real navy. In 1629 his forces attacked Batavia to drive out the Dutch, but superior Dutch naval forces held the city. Agung then turned east and fought the Balinese in Java.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Agung, sultan of Mataram

title: The Blind Naturalist of Ambon
text: In 1698 a blind German merchant, Georg Rumphius, sat in a whitewashed cottage on the spice island of Ambon, dictating detailed descriptions of crabs, sea snails, metals, stones and other rare things. He had lived most of his adult life there. He died alone on his island while the manuscript inched toward print, and in 1705 The Ambonese Curiosity Cabinet finally appeared in Amsterdam.

source.name: The New York Review of Books, Tim Flannery: Wonders of a Lost World

title: The King of Siam's Eclipse
text: King Mongkut of Siam worked out that a solar eclipse would cross his kingdom on August 18, 1868, and calculated that totality would last 6 minutes, 46 seconds. French astronomers found his prediction came within two seconds of their own. He watched from the jungle village of Wakor, but on the trip a mosquito gave him malaria, and he died six weeks after the expedition.

source.name: Science History Institute: The Eclipse That Killed a King (and May Have Saved a Kingdom)

title: A Garden That Grew an Industry
text: Singapore's botanic garden was created in 1859, first as a 'Pleasure Garden' in the English Landscape Style and later as an Economic Garden for plant research. Kew Gardens in Britain supplied the first rubber seedlings, but it was Singapore's garden that planted, developed and distributed them across much of Southeast Asia, helping plantation rubber expand. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Singapore Botanic Gardens

title: Tragedy Inside Batavia's Walls
text: For more than a century Chinese settlers had helped build Batavia, the Dutch East India Company's Asian headquarters. Then ecological decline, epidemics, runaway immigration and feuds among colonial officials broke that partnership. In October 1740, after a Chinese peasant uprising, the city's inhabitants massacred their Chinese neighbours inside the walls, looting house to house and sparing not even hospitals and prisons.

source.name: Leiden University: A Colonial Tragedy, The Chinese Massacre at Batavia, 1740 (Leonard Blussé)

title: A Governor Moves to Lifau
text: António Coelho Guerreiro was the first governor of Timor to actually live there, settling at Lifau, a sheltered bay favoured by merchants. A plan he ordered in 1702 shows a church of Saint Anthony and a hospital. He also had a large earth-and-stone fort built above the sea, guarding a community made up mainly of Portuguese mestizos and Chinese. Lifau stayed the centre of Portuguese power until 1769.

source.name: Heritage of Portuguese Influence (HPIP, Gulbenkian Foundation): Lifau

title: Bodawpaya Swallows Arakan
text: In 1784 King Bodawpaya of Myanmar invaded Arakan, the maritime kingdom on the Bay of Bengal, captured its king, Thamada, and deported more than 20,000 people as slaves. When Arakan became a province in 1785, Myanmar's border touched British India for the first time. Bodawpaya, who proclaimed himself a messianic Buddha, also began the Mingun pagoda, which would have stood 500 feet high if finished.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bodawpaya

title: The Price of a Throne
text: In 1794 the Siamese placed a refugee Cambodian prince, Eng, on the Cambodian throne. In exchange they took two provinces, Battambang and Siem Reap, which included the ruins of Angkor, and kept them until 1907. Squeezed between Siam and Vietnam, Cambodia went through 22 monarchs between 1603 and 1848, its kings losing territory and sovereignty by seeking foreign protection.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (David P. Chandler): Cambodia, Tai and Vietnamese hegemony

title: A Warehouseman's Secret Society
text: When Spain arrested the reformer José Rizal in 1892, shocked activists from a less privileged class quickly formed the Katipunan. Its leader, Andrés Bonifacio, was a self-educated warehouseman, and its aim was to expel the Spanish from the islands. For the first time, Filipino rebels combined nationalist goals with education. In August 1896 friars uncovered its plans, forcing an early revolt.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Gregorio C. Borlaza et al.): Philippines, The 19th century

title: One Vietnam, Two Governments
text: From about 1620 Vietnam was split in two. The Nguyen family, who had governed the south from Hue since 1558, refused to obey the Trinh princes who ran the north in the name of powerless Le emperors. For 50 years the Trinh tried to reconquer the south by force. Their last campaign failed in 1673, and a 100-year truce followed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Vietnam, Two divisions of Dai Viet

title: Vientiane's Great Stupa
text: King Setthathirath I (ruled 1548–71) moved the capital of the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang from Luang Prabang to Vientiane, a river port on a plain beside the Mekong, and drove back invasions around 1565 and 1570. The city's outstanding building, the stupa That Luang, dates from about 1566. Lao civil servants under Prince Phetsarath restored it during the French colonial period.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Vientiane

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Pierre-Bernard Lafont et al.): History of Laos
